narrative:
Based on the information available, there is a 96% chance you will leave your job in the near future. This high probability is the reason your promotion request was denied—promoting someone who is likely to depart soon carries significant risk for the organization, regardless of your qualifications.

Three factors weighed most heavily in this assessment. First, your total career experience of more than 11 years stands out. Among employees who stay, only about one in seven has this much experience. Professionals with your level of experience are often highly sought after and tend to have more confidence in their ability to find alternatives, which pushes the prediction toward departure.

Second, you indicated that you have received other job opportunities while working here. Only about 23% of employees who stay report this. Receiving outside offers signals that the market values your skills, making it more likely you will accept one of those opportunities rather than remain long-term.

Third, despite your extensive overall experience, you have only been in your current role for 1 to 5 years. While this tenure is common among stayers, combining long overall experience with relatively short time at this organization suggests you may not yet feel deeply rooted here, further increasing the likelihood that you would move on.

Considering these signals, the organization should recognize that your departure risk is driven largely by your strong market position and outside interest. If they wish to retain you, offering a promotion with meaningful career progression and addressing your broader job satisfaction concerns would be worthwhile. You may also reflect on whether staying aligns with your long-term goals.
